sentences.text: Cymbospondylus is an extinct genus of large ichthyosaurs.
These marine reptiles possessed flippers for limbs and a fin on their tail.
The smallest species of Cymbospondylus reached approximately 4 to 5 meters in length.
While the color of Cymbospondylus is unknown, some early ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark-colored, as evidenced by eumelanin pigments found in fossilized skin.
The best-known specimen of Cymbospondylus is UCMP 9950, an almost complete skeleton that has been used for size estimates since 1908.
Cymbospondylus had a curved skull with sharp teeth used to eat reptiles, primitive amphibians, and cephalopods like Ammonites.
The genus Cymbospondylus was described by Joseph Leidy in 1868.
The first fossils of Cymbospondylus were discovered in the 19th century in Nevada, United States.
Joseph Leidy described Cymbospondylus in 1868 based on vertebrae from Nevada, transmitted by geologist Josiah Dwight Whitney.
The name Cymbospondylus means "cupped vertebrae" in Ancient Greek, referring to the shape of the vertebrae.
More complete fossils of Cymbospondylus were discovered in the early 20th century by University of California expeditions and described by John Campbell Merriam in 1908.
It is agreed that Cymbospondylus is a basal member of the Ichthyosauria clade.
In a 2021 analysis, Cymbospondylus was placed at the base of Ichthyosauria, outside the derived Hueneosauria group.
C. youngorum is considered the most derived member of a Nevada clade, while C. buchseri sits at the base of the genus.
Recent studies classify Cymbospondylus as the type genus of the family Cymbospondylidae, rather than Shastasauridae.
Cymbospondylus lived during the Olenekian to Anisian stages of the Triassic period.
Some specimens of Cymbospondylus from Idaho and Svalbard date to the Olenekian stage of the Lower Triassic.
C. youngorum dates from the beginning of the Middle Triassic.
Established species of Cymbospondylus are known from fossil records in Nevada and Switzerland.
Cymbospondylus lived in marine ecosystems alongside bivalves, ammonites, Saurichthys, coelacanths, hybodonts, sauropterygians, and other ichthyosaurs.
In 2003, McGowan and Motani argued that the fossils attributed to C. piscosus lack distinctive characteristics to prove its validity.
McGowan and Motani suggested that the skeleton UCMP 9950 could be designated as a neotype for C. piscosus to resolve taxonomic issues.
Because no formal ICZN appeal has been established, the name C. petrinus is retained for the proposed neotype until further notice.
Researchers debated whether a skull attributed to C. petrinus actually belongs to C. nichollsi due to insufficient description of the specimen.
